summary: Surveys the state of the art and the remaining challenges of Internet of Things security. It notes that needs are well recognized and standards exist, for example CoAP secured with DTLS, but challenges remain. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Small connected gadgets need locks too. This document looks at what locks exist for them and which problems are still unsolved.

questions: internet of things security state of the art
what are the main threats to iot devices
subtitle: A survey of the threats facing Internet of Things devices, the protocols and guidelines that exist, and the security problems that remain open.

tldr.problem: IoT devices are often constrained, unattended, long-lived and physically exposed, and many were deployed with very limited security, so standard Internet security does not fit them well.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC walks through the lifecycle of a thing, lists eleven threats, reviews IP-based IoT protocols, security protocols and outside guidelines, and then discusses open challenges from resource limits to quantum resistance.
tldr.outcome: It is a reference for specification authors and implementers, not a standard. It ends with the challenges that need attention and asks authors to document clearly how their specifications address them.

today: RFC 8576 is an Informational RFC from the IRTF stream, published in April 2019, and has not been obsoleted or updated. Its survey reflects the state of the art at the time of writing, and the RFC itself notes that its references are representative and at varying levels of maturity.

sections.title: Scope and Origin
sections.content:
RFC 8576 is a product of the IRTF Thing-to-Thing Research Group (T2TRG). It gives an overview of security for the Internet of Things (IoT), meaning the interconnection of highly heterogeneous networked entities with communication patterns such as human-to-thing and thing-to-thing. The RFC says the document was reviewed over nearly six years, that it does not constitute a standard, and that IoT specifications can use it as a reference for security considerations.

It notes that IPv6 and CoAP (RFC 7252) are fundamental building blocks that allow connecting IoT hosts to the Internet, giving a homogeneous protocol ecosystem and simpler integration.
sections.plainLanguage: Many small gadgets now talk over the Internet. This paper is a guidebook to keeping them safe.

sections.title: The Thing Lifecycle
sections.content:
The RFC uses a Building Automation and Control system to show a generic lifecycle. A thing is manufactured, then installed and commissioned during bootstrapping, when its identity and secret keys may be provided. It then runs in operational mode and goes through occasional maintenance cycles where software is upgraded or applications are reconfigured, possibly needing rebootstrapping. At the end it is decommissioned, and may be recommissioned in another system under a different owner.

The RFC says security matters more for IoT because compromise can cause physical harm, can alter a manufacturer's device functionality, and can be misused at scale, for example in a DDoS attack. It calls the lifecycle a simplified model that could also include supply-chain, rebadging and forgotten-device phases.
sections.plainLanguage: A gadget is built, set up, used, fixed up now and then, and finally retired or given to a new owner. Each step has its own ways to go wrong.

sections.title: Threats and Managing Risk
sections.content:
The RFC lists eleven threats, in no particular order: vulnerable software, privacy threats, cloning of things, malicious substitution of things, eavesdropping, man-in-the-middle attacks, firmware attacks, extraction of private information, routing attacks, elevation of privilege, and denial of service. It cites the Mirai botnet, caused by things with well-known or easy-to-guess passwords.

Routing attacks it names include sinkhole, selective forwarding, wormhole and Sybil attacks. To manage risk it suggests a Business Impact Analysis, a Risk Assessment, a Privacy Impact Assessment, and procedures for incident reporting and mitigation, to be done when a system is created or significantly upgraded and reassessed regularly. It says risks classified as moderate or high must be mitigated.
sections.plainLanguage: Burglars might copy a gadget, swap it for a cheap one, listen in, or break its door. The paper lists these tricks so builders can plan against them.

sections.title: State of the Art
sections.content:
The RFC surveys IETF work for constrained devices: 6LoWPAN (RFC 4944), CoAP, the Resource Directory, SenML, the RPL routing protocol (RFC 6550), JSON and CBOR object formats with their signing and encryption variants (including COSE, RFC 8152), and LPWAN work. It also names industry efforts such as Thread, OCF and OMA LwM2M.

For security it covers IKEv2/IPsec, TLS, DTLS and HIP. CoAP defines three DTLS modes: PreSharedKey, RawPublicKey and Certificate. A TLS and DTLS 1.2 profile for constrained nodes is in RFC 7925. It also mentions ACE authorization based on OAuth 2.0 and OSCORE, which protects CoAP messages in COSE. Finally it lists thirteen sets of guidelines from bodies such as GSMA, BITAG, NIST, OWASP and ENISA, and notes that many IoT devices still have very limited security.
sections.plainLanguage: Plenty of tools and rulebooks already exist for protecting small gadgets. The trouble is that many makers do not use them.

sections.title: Challenges for a Secure IoT
sections.content:
Constraints come first: small packets (127 bytes in IEEE 802.15.4), little CPU, memory and energy make public key cryptography costly. Denial-of-service defenses such as return routability cookies are less effective on broadcast media or in meshes, and HIP puzzles can shut out weak devices when the attacker is powerful. End-to-end security conflicts with protocol translation at middleboxes, and the RFC reviews six approaches without finding a perfect one.

  • Groups: (D)TLS and IKEv2 cover only unicast, so group key establishment needs a solution.
  • Software updates: source authentication needs signature verification on small devices, and devices that cannot verify signatures should not be exposed to the Internet. Cryptographic agility is hard when hardware such as an AES128 coprocessor is relied on.
  • End-of-life, device behavior and testing: users may need ways to add trust anchors; Manufacturer Usage Description files (RFC 8520) are a first step for monitoring device behavior; testing of multi-vendor systems is an open question.
  • Quantum resistance: Shor's algorithm would break RSA and ECC, and long-lived devices face harvest-and-decrypt attacks.
  • Privacy and reverse engineering: secure elements and Physical Unclonable Functions can help protect keys and data.
sections.plainLanguage: Tiny gadgets have little brainpower and battery, last for years, and sit where anyone can reach them. That makes updates, secrets and privacy hard to get right.

sections.title: Conclusions and Next Steps
sections.content: The RFC names challenges needing particular attention: bootstrapping of security, group security, secure software updates, long-term security and quantum resistance, privacy protection, data leakage prevention, and trustworthy IoT operation. It asks authors of IoT specifications to put real effort into addressing these and to clearly document how they are addressed, which would reduce vulnerabilities in code written by implementers. Its own Security Considerations section says the entire memo deals with security issues.
sections.plainLanguage: The paper ends by asking everyone who writes the rules for gadgets to explain clearly how their rules keep people safe.
